newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus falls but surplus with U.S. up.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus falls but surplus with U.S. up.

text.p: Japan's merchandise trade surplus fell sharply in March but a rise in the surplus with the United States has economic analysts predicting more trade tensions between the two economic superpowers.
The Finance Ministry announced on Thursday that the overall surplus dropped 27 percent to 818.3 billion yen ($6.49 billion) in March from a year earlier.
But the surplus with the United States rose 11 percent year-on-year to 379.8 billion yen ($3.01 billion).
Even as the figures were coming out, U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers was warning of trade friction unless Japan became less reliant on exports and promotes growth from within.
"That is crucial to avoid a recurrence of the kind of strains that existed at some points in the past," he said in an evening speech to the Economic Strategy Institute in Washington on Wednesday.
The dollar fell to around 125.40 yen in Thursday morning trade in Tokyo after his remarks. It had inched up to near 126 yen earlier in the morning.

Summers comments are the latest in a barrage of warnings from top U.S. officials, including U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and House Speaker Newt Gingrich.

Economists said the large fall in the March overall surplus was due to a one-off jump in imports to satisfy strong consumer demand before Japan's sales tax was increased to five percent from three percent on April 1.
They said the trade surplus was definitely on a rising trend, with hefty increases expected in April, May and June as those months showed large declines last year.
Figures for the fiscal year, which ended on March 31, also released on Thursday, showed that the surplus fell 30 percent to 6.4 trillion yen ($50.7 billion) from the year before.
But economists polled in a recent Reuters quarterly survey said they expected it to expand this business year, to an average 10.5 trillion yen ($83.3 billion).
The March increase in the surplus with the United States also prompted some economists to predict a faster increase for the contentious bilateral surplus.
"As the overall trade surplus starts to rise, I think the surplus with the U.S. is going to rise faster than that," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Barings Japan.
Jerram also said he saw more pressure coming from Washington as policymakers focus on whether Japan is using a weaker yen to boost exports.
Previously, Washington was content with a strong dollar since it helped to keep down inflation.
"Now you're seeing the trade surplus increase and you're seeing pressure within the U.S. rise in terms of lobbying -- I think the U.S. is starting to change its stance," he said.

But Jason James, strategist at HSBC James Capel said that with the U.S. economy in pretty good shape and high employment levels, the United States could probably live with further rises for the time being.
He said concerns would grow if the surplus hits two percent of Japan's GDP. Currently the surplus is at 1.5 percent of GDP. ($1=126 yen)
